Bramble
BRAM-bul
noun
From the Old English brēmel, kin to brōm, the broom — a low, prickly, scrambling thorn-shrub of waste ground. In the AV it renders the Hebrew 'atad and the Greek batos: a bush that gives no timber, little fruit, and no shade worth the name.

Biblical Definition

The bramble is Scripture’s emblem of the unfit ruler. Its great text is Jotham’s parable, spoken from mount Gerizim after Abimelech had hired vain and light persons and slain his seventy brethren upon one stone (Jdg 9:5). The trees go forth to anoint a king. The olive will not leave its fatness, the fig its sweetness, the vine its wine — each has a use, and each knows it. “Then said all the trees unto the bramble, Come thou, and reign over us” (Jdg 9:14). Only the useless bush accepts, and its acceptance is a threat dressed as an invitation: “If in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and put your trust in my shadow: and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon” (Jdg 9:15). A bramble has no shadow to trust in; a bramble is exactly what fire runs through fastest. Both halves came true, for within three years fire came out from Abimelech and from Shechem and devoured them each of the other (Jdg 9:20, 56–57). Our Lord uses the same shrub for a different edge: “every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes” (Luk 6:44). Nature governs fruit; a bramble cannot be argued into bearing grapes. And where judgment has fallen, the bramble takes the ground: “thorns shall come up in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof” (Isa 34:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

A prickly scrambling shrub of waste ground, useless for timber or fruit; the emblem of the unfit ruler.

BRAMBLE, a prickly shrub of the waste places, yielding neither timber nor good fruit.

From the Old English brēmel, kin to brōm, the broom.

In the AV it renders the Hebrew 'atad and the Greek batos.

Jotham made it the king of the trees in his parable (Jdg 9:14–15).

Christ named it as a bush from which no man gathers grapes (Luk 6:44).

Key Scripture

Jdg 9:14 — "Then said all the trees unto the bramble, Come thou, and reign over us."

Jdg 9:15 — "And the bramble said unto the trees, If in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and put your trust in my shadow: and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon."

Luk 6:44 — "For every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes."

Isa 34:13 — "And thorns shall come up in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof: and it shall be an habitation of dragons, and a court for owls."

Modern Corruption

The bush that campaigns for the crown — the pattern of every self-appointed leader whose shade is imaginary and whose fire is not.

expand to see more

The corruption is self-appointed leadership, in the state and in the church alike, and Jotham drew its portrait three thousand years before the age of the platform. The fruitful trees decline the crown because they have work; the barren bush seeks it because it has nothing else. So it goes still. The man with a genuine calling to a real labour is reluctant to be made much of; the man with no fruit is available at once, and he arrives with the bramble’s two promises — a shade he does not possess and a fire he certainly does. The church knows this figure well: the leader who gathers a personal following rather than a congregation, who binds men to himself instead of feeding them, who threatens and flatters by turns, and who at last consumes the very people who anointed him. Paul warned the Ephesian elders that such men would rise “of your own selves… speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30).

The remedy is the qualification lists God has already given, and the plurality that guards them. Scripture does not ask who wants the office; it asks what a man is: blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, of good behaviour, apt to teach, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre, not a novice, ruling his own house well and having a good report of them which are without (1Ti 3:2–7; Tit 1:5–9). Those are all fruit tests, and they are exactly the test Christ named — “every tree is known by his own fruit” (Luk 6:44). That word cuts twice. It disqualifies the bramble from ruling, and it disqualifies the barren professor from presuming, against the easy-believism that assures a man of heaven on the strength of a decision while his life bears grapes of Sodom. Elders are to be tried before they serve (1Ti 3:10), and every man is to examine himself (2Co 13:5); the bush that bears no grapes is a bramble, whatever it calls itself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word names a prickly, fruitless shrub of the waste — no timber, no grapes, no shade.

expand to see more

Bramble — Old English brēmel, kin to brōm, the broom.

It is a low, thorny, scrambling shrub of ruined and waste ground.

In the AV it renders the Hebrew 'atad and the Greek batos.

In Jotham’s parable it alone accepts the crown the fruitful trees refuse (Jdg 9:14).

It offers a shadow it has not, and a fire it has (Jdg 9:15).

Usage

"The olive, fig, and vine had work to do; only the bramble had time to be king."

"Put your trust in my shadow — the promise of a bush that casts none."

"Of a bramble bush gather they grapes? Nature settles fruit, and fruit settles the man."
